title: Bună dimineața!
source: Limba care ne unește, nivelul I — Lecția 1

spoken_layer.book: El este bărbat. Ea este femeie.
spoken_layer.spoken: El e bărbat. Ea e femeie.
spoken_layer.note: The single most frequent gap between written and spoken Romanian. Este is correct and never wrong, but in conversation almost everyone says e. Teach este in the drill, because that is the form the book builds on, and teach e as the one you will actually hear.
Spoken Romanian drops the final -l of the definite article: domnul becomes domnu', băiatul becomes băiatu'. This is ordinary neutral speech, not sloppiness. Feminine -a is unaffected.
The standard thing to say when introduced. The chapter teaches greetings and nationalities but never this, and it is the phrase a real first meeting cannot do without. Teach as a fixed chunk.

spoken_layer.gloss: How are you? — polite, to one person or several
spoken_layer.note: Follows the greeting almost automatically. Grammar is well beyond lesson one, so deliver it whole and do not analyse it.

The book presents all three flat, as if interchangeable. They are not. Bună ziua to a stranger, an official, anyone older. Bună with someone your own age you have met. Salut only with friends. Getting this wrong is more noticeable than a grammar mistake.

spoken_layer.gloss: Well... — the closest thing to Russian ну
spoken_layer.note: Opens a hesitant or qualified answer. Neutral: fine with colleagues and shopkeepers. Păi, nu sunt din Chișinău. — Well, I'm not from Chișinău.
Formally means therefore, but in speech it fills pauses and restarts sentences the way English so does. Extremely common; can be drawn out while thinking.
Used to concede a point or correct yourself mid-sentence. Neutral register. Useful early because it buys time without sounding uncertain.
The book is from Chișinău, 2003, and offers both spellings. The î forms are dated and marked in Romania. Use only the u forms.

segments.text: Nu. Sunt din Bălți. Sunt moldovean.
Ah, scuzați! Domnișoara Elena. Dumneavoastră sunteți din Chișinău?
Da. Dar nu sunt moldoveancă. Sunt ucraineancă.
Iar eu sunt din Chișinău. Sunt moldoveancă.
Three people and a register, first morning of a language course. You caught a name or two — that is the right amount on a first listen. We come back to it at the end.
Four letters first. Only the four that turned up in what you just heard.
Ă, an A wearing a little bowl. A dull vowel, the -er at the end of 'water'. In bărbat, a man.
Ș, an S with a comma under it. Just 'sh'. In domnișoară, miss.
Ț, a T with a comma under it. 'ts', as at the end of 'cats'. In dimineața, morning.
And Î or Â — one sound, two spellings. Nothing like it in English: say 'ee' with your tongue pulled back. In în, meaning in.
Now the words, each one inside a phrase. Say every phrase out loud in the gap. Out loud — thinking it does not count.
Three ways to address someone. You heard all three during the roll call.

And when a title comes before a name, it grows an ending: domnul Radu, doamna Elena, domnișoara Elena. That ending is Romanian's word for 'the', and it attaches to the back of the word instead of standing in front of it. Take it as a whole phrase for now.
Nationalities. Listen for the pattern rather than memorising ten separate words.
I am Moldovan — said by a man.
I am Moldovan — said by a woman.
There it is: the men's form ends in nothing in particular, the women's adds -că. Moldovean, moldoveancă. Ucrainean, ucraineancă. That one rule covers most of the list.
Two very small words that people mix up forever.
Din is from. În is in. Once more, slowly.
El este din Moldova, iar ea este din Ucraina.
He is from Moldova, and she is from Ukraine.
El este din Moldova, iar ea este din Ucraina.
Sunt rus, dar el este român.
I am Russian, but he is Romanian.
Sunt rus, dar el este român.
Everything in this episode runs on one verb: a fi, to be. Six forms.
For the negative, put nu in front and change nothing else.
Now something worth stopping for. Listen to what Radu actually said when Dana asked where he was from.
Nu. Sunt din Bălți. Sunt moldovean.
Not eu sunt din Bălți. Just sunt din Bălți. Romanian usually leaves the pronoun out, because the verb ending already tells you who is speaking. Sunt can only mean I am.
The pronoun comes back when you are pointing at someone in particular. Dana reads a name, and Radu answers:
Yes, that is me. There the eu is the whole point.
So: drop it for plain statements, keep it for contrast. The drill below uses full forms because those need practice. In speech, let them go.
Six phrases for arriving and leaving.
One more pair. Dumneavoastră is the respectful you — Dana used it with everyone on her list. Dumneata is a middle setting, polite but warmer.
Note that dumneavoastră takes sunteți, the plural form, even for one person — the same move French makes with vous.
Last section, and it is not from the textbook. That book was written in Chișinău in 2003. It teaches correct Romanian, not always spoken Romanian. So: what a Bucharest mouth actually produces.
The book says el este, ea este. Correct, always. But listen:
Just e. The commonest gap between written and spoken Romanian. Keep drilling este — the book builds on it — but expect e.
We taught domnul Radu. In speech that final L falls off.
Domnu', not domnul. Ordinary neutral speech, not sloppiness. Feminine doamna keeps its ending.
Now the phrase our roll call should have had. On being introduced:
Grammar far beyond this lesson. Take it whole.
And two ways to stall while you think.
And deci — officially therefore, in speech just like English 'so'. Stretch it as long as you need.
Both neutral. Safe with a colleague, in a shop, with a stranger.
This is the part that does the work. I say it in English, you say it in Romanian out loud, then you hear it. Answer before you are sure — guessing and being corrected is what makes it stick.
I am Moldovan — you are a man.
I am Moldovan — you are a woman.
You are from Bulgaria — speaking to several people.
They are from Moldova — a group of men.
He is not English, he is Gagauz.
El nu este englez, el este găgăuz.
Are you from Ukraine? Politely, to one person.
He is a man, she is a woman.
El este bărbat, ea este femeie.
He is from Moldova, and she is from Ukraine.
El este din Moldova, iar ea este din Ucraina.
He is a man — the way you would actually say it.
Well... I am not from Chișinău.
Here is the reading passage from the lesson itself. Slowly first.
Eu sunt Ion. Sunt din Moldova.
Și el este din Moldova, iar ea este din Ucraina.
Tu ești din Chișinău. Noi suntem din Bulgaria.
Voi sunteți din Rusia. Dar ei? Ei sunt din America.
El este Radu, iar ea este Dana.
El este bărbat, ea este femeie. Noi suntem din Moldova.
Eu sunt Ion. Sunt din Moldova.
Și el este din Moldova, iar ea este din Ucraina.
Tu ești din Chișinău. Noi suntem din Bulgaria.
Voi sunteți din Rusia. Dar ei? Ei sunt din America.
El este Radu, iar ea este Dana.
El este bărbat, ea este femeie. Noi suntem din Moldova.
Back to the roll call. Same recording, same speed. Nothing about it has changed.
Nu. Sunt din Bălți. Sunt moldovean.
Ah, scuzați! Domnișoara Elena. Dumneavoastră sunteți din Chișinău?
Da. Dar nu sunt moldoveancă. Sunt ucraineancă.
Iar eu sunt din Chișinău. Sunt moldoveancă.
Every word of that was built from this one lesson. Twenty-four words and one verb.
One thing before the next episode. Say your own line out loud — where you are from, what you are. Start with sunt, and leave the eu off. Pe curând!
